chunks: Al-Kafi: Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from A'sim ibn Humayd, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I discussed with Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding what they narrate about the vision (of God). He said: The sun is one part out of seventy parts of the light of the Chair. The Chair is one part out of seventy parts of the light of the Throne. The Throne is one part out of seventy parts of the light of the Veil. The Veil is one part out of seventy parts of the light of the Covering. If they are truthful, let them fill their eyes with the sun, with no cloud below it.
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia theological argument against the physical vision of God based on the light of the sun?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) employs a cosmological analogy of light intensity to refute the possibility of seeing God with physical eyes, arguing that if the sun is merely a fraction of the light of the Throne, the Divine Light would be overwhelming. This hadith is central to the Shia doctrine of *Tajassum* (incarnation/embodiment) vs. *Tanzih* (transcendence), emphasizing that physical vision (*ru'ya*) is limited to created forms and cannot encompass the uncreated Essence. The reference to the 'Covering' (*Al-Sitr*) highlights the veiling of the Divine Essence from direct sensory perception, a key concept in Shia theological discourse.
